title: Northstar AI x Redwood Inference — usage + rate limit follow-up
summary: Outbound follow-up triggered by sustained spend growth and repeated 429 (rate limit) hits on Redwood Hosted API. Northstar AI described production chat + summarization workloads with bursty concurrency (weekday spikes) and latency targets that are increasingly missed during bursts. Redwood proposed near-term quota adjustments and request shaping (streaming, retries, batching) while scoping Redwood Dedicated as the likely next step for predictable throughput. Next steps include sharing a sizing worksheet, getting Northstar’s request/latency distribution, and scheduling a technical benchmark session to validate dedicated capacity + autoscaling policy.
topics: Reason for outreach: sustained spend + 429/rate-limit events
Workload overview: customer-facing chat, internal summarization jobs, embeddings for retrieval
Traffic pattern: bursts, concurrency spikes, regional mix
SLOs: p95 latency and timeout behavior, streaming usage
Current mitigations: retries, queueing, backoff; pain points in prod incidents
Dedicated vs Hosted: capacity isolation, throughput predictability, autoscaling and burst policies
Security and procurement: SOC 2, audit logs, data retention expectations (light touch)
Next steps: data needed for sizing + benchmark plan
questions: What are your current p50/p95 latency targets and what do you see during peak?
Are the 429s happening on a single API key/project or across multiple services?
What is your typical prompt+completion token distribution (short chat vs long summaries)?
Do you need single-tenant isolation primarily for reliability (throughput) or for security/compliance?
Any constraints on region (EU-only) or customer data residency requirements?
action_items: Redwood (Stephanie Nguyen): Send Northstar a dedicated sizing worksheet + initial pricing guardrails for Dedicated capacity by 2025-02-28
Redwood (Markus Klein): Propose a benchmark plan (models, concurrency targets, success criteria) and schedule a 60-min technical session by 2025-03-03
Northstar AI (Evan Brooks): Share last 7 days of request distribution (RPS/concurrency), top routes, and observed 429 timestamps by 2025-03-03
Northstar AI (Priya Desai): Confirm near-term timeline for capacity decision (March vs April) and whether procurement/security will require formal packet by 2025-03-05
Redwood (Stephanie Nguyen): Coordinate with Billing/Quotas team on a temporary quota increase while Dedicated is evaluated by 2025-02-28
next_steps: Northstar sends usage/latency distribution + 429 examples (timestamps, routes, model IDs).
Redwood shares Dedicated sizing + rough commit bands and suggests a pilot configuration (GPU type, region, autoscaling).
Schedule technical benchmark / deep dive with Northstar platform engineer + Redwood SE.
If benchmark is positive, create a mutual action plan for a 2–3 week Dedicated PoC with success criteria (p95 latency at peak concurrency, error rate, cost per 1M tokens).
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Northstar AI x Redwood Inference — usage + rate limit follow-up
Date: 2025-02-27
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 38 minutes

Attendees
- Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood Inference) — Sales
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference) — Solutions Engineering
- Priya Desai (Northstar AI) — Head of ML
- Evan Brooks (Northstar AI) — Platform Engineer
- Sara Kim (Northstar AI) — Engineering Manager

---
Summary (auto-generated)
Northstar AI discussed recent scale-up on Redwood Hosted API, including sustained spend growth and repeated 429 responses during peak periods. Redwood reviewed likely causes (quota ceilings + bursty concurrency) and outlined options: short-term quota adjustments and request shaping, plus scoping Redwood Dedicated for predictable throughput. Agreed to share sizing inputs and schedule a benchmark session.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Rate limit errors (429)
- Concurrency spikes and latency SLOs
- Dedicated capacity scoping
- Benchmark plan + next steps

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to send sizing worksheet and Dedicated overview
- Northstar to share traffic distribution and timestamps of incidents
- Schedule technical benchmark session

---

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I know this one was a little bit of an “out of the blue” follow-up. I’m Stephanie, I run a chunk of our NA accounts here at Redwood.

[00:10] Stephanie Nguyen: The reason we reached out is, we saw Northstar’s usage has been steadily climbing over the last few weeks, which is awesome, and we also saw a pattern of rate-limit hits, like repeated 429s. So this is really to understand what you’re building, what’s breaking, and whether we should talk about dedicated capacity or changes on the hosted side.

[00:29] Priya Desai: Yeah, makes sense. We got the email and it actually lined up because we had… not an incident, but like a very stressful afternoon last Thursday.

[00:38] Sara Kim: Two afternoons. (laughs)

[00:41] Stephanie Nguyen: (laughs) Okay, good timing then. And Markus is here with me, he’s our SE lead on inference performance, so he can go deep on what we can do.

[00:51] Markus Klein: Hey all.

[00:53] Evan Brooks: Hey.

[00:54] Priya Desai: Hi Markus.

[01:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Before we jump in, quick agenda: I want to understand the workload and what “good” looks like—latency, throughput, regions. Markus can ask some technical questions. Then we can talk options, including Dedicated. Does that work?

[01:14] Priya Desai: Yep.

[01:16] Sara Kim: Sounds good.

[01:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Priya, do you want to give the 60-second overview? What’s Northstar shipping with Redwood today?

[01:27] Priya Desai: Sure. We’re an analytics copilot for… mostly B2B SaaS finance teams. The main thing is a chat interface where customers ask questions about their data, plus we do background summarization of reports and alerts.

[01:44] Priya Desai: The chat is customer-facing, so latency is the big deal. Summaries are more batchy, but they can pile up.

[01:55] Markus Klein: Are those two separate services calling the API or the same backend?

[02:00] Evan Brooks: Same backend, different routes. We have separate API keys in Redwood for staging vs prod, but prod is shared.

[02:08] Stephanie Nguyen: Got it. And roughly what’s traffic like—RPS or concurrency?

[02:14] Evan Brooks: It’s very spiky. Average is fine. But during business hours on the US East coast we’ll see like… we can hit, I don’t know, 80 to 120 concurrent requests if a bunch of customers are on.

[02:29] Evan Brooks: Then the batch jobs kick in and we’re doing these long-ish summaries, and that’s when it gets ugly.

[02:37] Sara Kim: The symptoms for us are timeouts and then retries, and then we amplify it ourselves. Like, we’re trying to be careful but you know how it goes.

[02:48] Markus Klein: Yeah, retry storms. Totally.

[02:51] Stephanie Nguyen: And the 429s you saw—are those coming from Redwood directly, or from your own gateway?

[02:57] Evan Brooks: From Redwood. Response body is rate limit exceeded. I can pull an example later.

[03:05] Markus Klein: That’s helpful. Typically that’s either the plan limit or a per-minute/per-second cap that’s getting hit during bursts.

[03:12] Stephanie Nguyen: When you hit the limit, is it a big block of time? Like five minutes of pain? Or just scattered?

[03:18] Evan Brooks: It tends to cluster. Like we’ll have a ten-minute window where it’s bad. Then it recovers.

[03:26] Priya Desai: And the frustrating part is it’s correlated with our important customers being online.

[03:31] Stephanie Nguyen: Yeah. Understood.

[03:35] Markus Klein: Can we talk about models and token shapes? Like what model are you primarily using in Redwood?

[03:42] Priya Desai: We’re on… I might mis-say it. “Llama 3… 70B instruct”? I think that’s the one. And then we do embeddings too.

[03:52] Evan Brooks: It’s the 70B chat model, yes. For embeddings we use your default embedding endpoint.

[03:58] Markus Klein: Perfect. For the chat, are you streaming responses back to the UI?

[04:04] Sara Kim: Yes, mostly. We turned on streaming because it helped perceived latency.

[04:09] Markus Klein: Great. And the long summaries—what’s the rough prompt + completion length?

[04:15] Priya Desai: Prompts can be big because we stuff context. Like maybe 8k to 20k tokens input, then output a few hundred to 1k.

[04:26] Markus Klein: Okay. And chat is shorter?

[04:28] Priya Desai: Chat is, like, 1k to 4k in, a couple hundred out.

[04:34] Stephanie Nguyen: That token shape matters a lot for throughput and for batching.

[04:38] Evan Brooks: Yeah, we kind of suspected.

[04:41] Markus Klein: Do you have any guardrails on max tokens? Like do you cap the long summary jobs?

[04:46] Evan Brooks: We do now. After last week we lowered max output tokens. But it’s still a lot.

[04:54] Sara Kim: We also added queueing for batch jobs, but the problem is our customers expect “near real time” summaries. So we can’t push it too far.

[05:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Makes sense. Let me reflect what I’m hearing: you’re growing, chat is latency-sensitive, and during peak you get 429s plus p95 latency climbing. Correct?

[05:15] Priya Desai: Yep.

[05:16] Evan Brooks: Yes.

[05:18] Stephanie Nguyen: What are your SLOs today? Like p95 target.

[05:22] Sara Kim: We tell customers “a few seconds” which is vague. Internally we aim for under 2.5 seconds to first token for chat, and under, like, 8 seconds for the whole thing.

[05:35] Markus Klein: Time-to-first-token and total time, got it. And what do you see during those bad windows?

[05:41] Evan Brooks: TTFT can jump to 6, 7 seconds. And some requests just time out at 30 seconds because of our gateway.

[05:49] Priya Desai: Then we get customer tickets.

[05:52] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep.

[05:55] Markus Klein: When you’re seeing 429s, do you also see higher latency on the successful requests? Or is it purely rejections?

[06:01] Evan Brooks: Both. It’s like the system is saturated. So latency goes up, then we start getting 429s.

[06:09] Markus Klein: That pattern is consistent with hitting your throughput quota, and then the queues get long.

[06:14] Stephanie Nguyen: I want to ask a slightly commercial question but it’s really operational: is this a case where you mainly need higher limits on hosted, or do you need isolation and predictability, which is where Dedicated comes in?

[06:28] Priya Desai: Predictability. We don’t want to be the noisy neighbor or whatever. We don’t want to be impacted by other folks.

[06:35] Sara Kim: Also we don’t want our batch jobs to ruin chat. Like we want some separation.

[06:40] Markus Klein: That’s actually a big one. On Dedicated you can set routing policies so batch jobs go to one pool, chat goes to another, or at least set concurrency limits per route.

[06:52] Evan Brooks: That sounds like what we need.

[06:55] Stephanie Nguyen: Got it. And any security or compliance drivers? Or mostly performance?

[07:01] Priya Desai: Mostly performance for now. We do get security questionnaires. SOC2 comes up, SSO comes up. But we’re not in, like, healthcare.

[07:11] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood.

[07:13] Markus Klein: Region-wise, where are your users? Are you mostly US?

[07:17] Evan Brooks: Mostly US, some EU. But we’re okay serving EU from US today. We may need EU region later.

[07:26] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. That gives flexibility.

[07:29] Markus Klein: Can I ask what you’re using besides Redwood? Any fallback provider?

[07:34] Sara Kim: We tried OpenAI early days. Cost got out of hand for our context sizes.

[07:40] Priya Desai: We also looked at Bedrock because procurement likes AWS, but the performance was… variable for what we needed.

[07:48] Evan Brooks: And we tested Together.ai briefly. Similar story: it worked but we didn’t want to stitch too many providers.

[07:56] Markus Klein: Makes sense.

[08:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Totally. Our goal is to avoid you needing a bunch of fallbacks for basic reliability.

[08:06] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s dig into last Thursday. What happened exactly?

[08:10] Sara Kim: We had a webinar, like a marketing event, so we had more customers trying the product at once. And the batch summarization job also ran because of the new signups. We got a flood of chat requests.

[08:25] Sara Kim: We saw rising latency, then the 429s started. We rate-limited ourselves, but then customers saw “try again” messages.

[08:34] Evan Brooks: And our retry logic isn’t perfect; it retries too quickly sometimes.

[08:40] Markus Klein: Yep. If you can share one or two request IDs or timestamps we can correlate with our logs. Even if it’s just a CSV of timestamps.

[08:49] Evan Brooks: We can do that.

[08:51] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[08:53] Markus Klein: Also, are you doing any client-side parallelization? Like do you fire multiple completions per user action?

[09:01] Priya Desai: Sometimes. We do one main answer, plus we do a “citations” extraction call in parallel. And occasionally we run a rerank.

[09:12] Markus Klein: Okay. So one UI action could be 2 to 3 calls.

[09:16] Sara Kim: Correct.

[09:18] Markus Klein: That’s important for concurrency. Because “50 active users” might be “150 calls” if you parallelize.

[09:24] Evan Brooks: Yep.

[09:27] Stephanie Nguyen: This is actually why the signal pinged us. Not just spend, but we see consistent high concurrency periods and then 429s.

[09:36] Priya Desai: Yeah, the spend part wasn’t a surprise. We’ve been growing.

[09:41] Stephanie Nguyen: Congrats on that, by the way.

[09:44] Priya Desai: Thanks.

[09:46] Markus Klein: On the short-term side, there are two buckets: (1) quota/limit adjustments so you don’t hit 429 as easily, and (2) request shaping so you don’t create self-inflicted spikes.

[09:58] Markus Klein: On the longer-term side, Dedicated gives you an isolated pool so you can guarantee throughput and set policies per route.

[10:07] Evan Brooks: How quickly can you adjust quotas? Like is that a support ticket thing?

[10:12] Stephanie Nguyen: We can do it pretty quickly, especially for accounts at your usage level. I can coordinate internally today. It won’t solve every saturation issue, but it can remove the hard ceiling.

[10:25] Sara Kim: That would help. Even if it just buys us time.

[10:28] Stephanie Nguyen: Exactly.

[10:30] Priya Desai: We also don’t want to pay a ton more just for higher limits, if Dedicated is the right thing anyway.

[10:38] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep. So what I propose is: we do a temporary increase so you’re not falling over, and in parallel we scope Dedicated and see if the economics and performance make sense.

[10:49] Markus Klein: For Dedicated sizing, we need: your token per second needs, concurrency distribution, and token length distribution. Not perfect, but directional.

[10:58] Evan Brooks: We can pull that from our logs. We track prompt size and completion size.

[11:03] Markus Klein: Great.

[11:06] Stephanie Nguyen: Priya, timeline-wise, when do you need this stabilized? Like are you okay with “in March” or do you need “next week”?

[11:14] Priya Desai: Honestly, next week would be great. But realistically, we can do a decision in March.

[11:21] Sara Kim: We have another event mid-March.

[11:24] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. Let’s aim to have a recommendation well before that.

[11:29] Markus Klein: If we set up a benchmark session early next week, we can turn sizing around quickly.

[11:35] Evan Brooks: What does the benchmark entail? Like do we run load tests against your endpoint?

[11:41] Markus Klein: Yeah. We’ll propose a few scenarios. For example: chat workload at concurrency X with your typical token lengths, measure TTFT and p95. Then a mixed workload scenario: chat plus background summaries. And we can test policy controls like max concurrency for batch.

[12:00] Markus Klein: The key is defining success criteria so it’s not subjective.

[12:05] Sara Kim: That would be good.

[12:07] Priya Desai: We also care about cost. Like, we moved to you because cost per token was better than OpenAI for our long contexts.

[12:15] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep. Dedicated changes the pricing model—more like reserved capacity—so unit cost can improve, but you’re committing to capacity. We’ll walk through it with guardrails.

[12:28] Evan Brooks: Does Dedicated mean we still call the same API? Or different base URL?

[12:32] Markus Klein: Same API surface. You get a dedicated “deployment” in our system, but your integration is basically the same. You’ll have a separate project and endpoint config. Your code changes are minimal.

[12:45] Evan Brooks: Nice.

[12:46] Sara Kim: And can we isolate batch vs chat, like Priya mentioned?

[12:51] Markus Klein: Yes. You can do per-route limits and priority. Some folks do separate deployments for batch and chat. Or one deployment with queue policies.

[13:03] Priya Desai: What about fallbacks if the dedicated pool is full? Like can it spill over to hosted?

[13:10] Markus Klein: Good question. We can configure fallback policies, but generally if you buy dedicated, we size it so you don’t need to spill. For rare spikes, we can discuss burst capacity or a limited fallback.

[13:24] Stephanie Nguyen: It’s a tradeoff: strict isolation vs elastic overflow.

[13:28] Evan Brooks: Makes sense.

[13:30] Stephanie Nguyen: Let me ask: are these spikes predictable? Like every day 11am PT? Or random?

[13:36] Sara Kim: It’s somewhat predictable—weekday mornings and afternoons. But events create big spikes.

[13:44] Priya Desai: Also month-end is heavier because finance teams.

[13:48] Markus Klein: Month-end, yep.

[13:51] Markus Klein: On the request shaping side: do you have exponential backoff on retries? And do you cap retries?

[13:58] Evan Brooks: We have exponential backoff but it’s… not aggressive enough. It starts at 200ms.

[14:05] Markus Klein: That’s pretty tight. You might want to start at 1-2 seconds for 429s. And jitter.

[14:11] Evan Brooks: Yeah.

[14:13] Sara Kim: We were trying to keep UI snappy.

[14:15] Markus Klein: Totally. But if it’s 429, the system is basically telling you “not now.” If you hammer it, it gets worse.

[14:24] Stephanie Nguyen: Markus can send best practices on retry/backoff for rate limits.

[14:29] Evan Brooks: That would help.

[14:31] Priya Desai: Another question: can we get visibility on our limits? Because right now it’s a bit opaque. We just find out when it breaks.

[14:39] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes. In the Console we have quota dashboards, and we can also expose the effective limits for your project. If that’s not showing up, we should fix it.

[14:51] Markus Klein: There’s also per-route analytics: error rate and latency. If you’re not using it, we can walk you through.

[14:57] Sara Kim: We use it a bit, but we mostly rely on Datadog.

[15:01] Markus Klein: That’s fine. We can integrate tracing hooks too, but not necessary for this.

[15:06] Stephanie Nguyen: Quick check: is anyone else joining from your side? Security, procurement?

[15:11] Priya Desai: Not yet. If we go Dedicated, procurement will show up.

[15:16] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay.

[15:18] Markus Klein: For Dedicated, would you need VPC / private connectivity? Or okay over public internet with auth?

[15:26] Evan Brooks: Public is okay for now. Longer-term maybe private networking, but it’s not a requirement today.

[15:33] Priya Desai: We’re on AWS, so VPC peering is an option but not urgent.

[15:38] Markus Klein: Great. That makes the timeline faster.

[15:41] Stephanie Nguyen: Do you have any data residency constraints today?

[15:45] Priya Desai: Not strict. Maybe later for EU customers. But today we’re okay.

[15:52] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay.

[15:54] Markus Klein: One more technical question: are you using function calling / tool calling? Or plain text?

[16:00] Priya Desai: We do a little. Mostly we have the model produce a JSON-ish structure to call internal tools.

[16:07] Markus Klein: Got it.

[16:09] Sara Kim: The JSON sometimes breaks. But that’s not today’s topic.

[16:13] Markus Klein: (laughs) Yeah, separate call.

[16:16] Stephanie Nguyen: (laughs) We can help there too.

[16:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay, so in terms of next steps: Evan, you said you can share timestamps and maybe a couple example responses?

[16:26] Evan Brooks: Yes. I can export a log sample. We have route, status code, latency, prompt tokens, completion tokens.

[16:34] Markus Klein: Perfect. If you can include concurrency estimate at the time, even better.

[16:39] Evan Brooks: We have queue depth metrics. I’ll include that.

[16:43] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[16:45] Priya Desai: What do you need from me?

[16:48] Stephanie Nguyen: Mostly timeline and stakeholders. You mentioned mid-March event. If Dedicated is the direction, we’ll want to line up a PoC quickly.

[16:59] Priya Desai: Okay.

[17:01] Markus Klein: For the PoC, success criteria could be: “chat TTFT p95 under 2.5 seconds at 120 concurrency” or whatever your peak is. And “429s eliminated.” Plus cost targets.

[17:15] Sara Kim: Yeah, eliminating 429s is the big one.

[17:18] Evan Brooks: And more stable latency, even if average is the same.

[17:22] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[17:24] Stephanie Nguyen: On our side, I’ll also look at your current plan limits and see if a temporary uplift can be approved today.

[17:32] Evan Brooks: Thank you.

[17:34] Priya Desai: Is that going to require us to change anything? Like new contract?

[17:38] Stephanie Nguyen: No, not for a temporary adjustment. Dedicated would be a contract, but quota changes on hosted are operational.

[17:47] Priya Desai: Great.

[17:49] Markus Klein: Another small thing: for batch summaries, you might consider lower priority or running them with a smaller model if quality allows. Do you need the 70B for summaries?

[18:03] Priya Desai: Maybe not. We use it because it’s “good enough” for everything and we didn’t want complexity.

[18:10] Sara Kim: But if it saves us, we can consider a smaller one for batch.

[18:14] Markus Klein: That could reduce cost and reduce contention. We can test that in the benchmark.

[18:22] Evan Brooks: That’s interesting.

[18:24] Stephanie Nguyen: This is where Redwood Optimize recommendations can help, but we don’t need to overcomplicate today.

[18:31] Priya Desai: Okay.

[18:33] Stephanie Nguyen: Markus, anything else you want to ask before we wrap?

[18:37] Markus Klein: Two quick ones: (1) do you use caching at all? Like prompt prefix caching for repeated system prompts?

[18:44] Evan Brooks: Not explicitly. We just send the whole prompt.

[18:48] Markus Klein: Okay. There are some built-in caching behaviors depending on the deployment, but we can also help you structure prompts so cache hits are more likely. That can improve throughput.

[19:00] Evan Brooks: Nice.

[19:02] Markus Klein: (2) Any hard timeout in your app that we should account for during load tests?

[19:07] Sara Kim: API gateway is 30 seconds. UI shows “still working” after 10 seconds but we don’t keep the connection forever.

[19:15] Markus Klein: Perfect, we’ll test within those.

[19:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[19:20] (crosstalk)

[19:21] Priya Desai: Can you share anything on what Dedicated looks like in terms of management? Like do we have to manage GPUs?

[19:28] Stephanie Nguyen: No. We manage the infrastructure. You’re reserving a pool, but you’re not SSH-ing into anything. You manage it via Console: model version, routing rules, autoscaling policy.

[19:41] Markus Klein: And we’ll set it up with you. You’ll have an assigned SE for the PoC.

[19:46] Priya Desai: Great.

[19:48] Sara Kim: What about SLAs?

[19:50] Stephanie Nguyen: Dedicated includes SLA options—uptime and response-time targets depending on the tier. We can share the specifics once we confirm the right tier.

[20:01] Sara Kim: Okay.

[20:03] Evan Brooks: So practically, the next meeting is a benchmark planning session?

[20:08] Markus Klein: Yep. I’ll send a calendar hold for 60 minutes. We’ll come with a proposed test plan and data requests.

[20:15] Stephanie Nguyen: And I’ll send a recap email with the action items. Evan, if you can send the log sample by Monday, that would be perfect.

[20:25] Evan Brooks: Yep, Monday is fine.

[20:27] Priya Desai: Works.

[20:29] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Before we close, any concerns about moving to Dedicated? Like internal resistance?

[20:36] Priya Desai: Mostly budget. We need to justify commit. But if it fixes reliability, it’s easier.

[20:43] Sara Kim: And engineering time. We can’t do a huge migration.

[20:46] Markus Klein: It shouldn’t be huge. Most customers keep the same API integration and just swap credentials/endpoint config. If you want route-based separation, that’s small code changes.

[20:59] Evan Brooks: That’s good.

[21:01] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay.

[21:03] (brief pause)

[21:04] Stephanie Nguyen: I’ll stop us here and give you time back. Thanks again. We’ll follow up with the worksheet, quota update, and a benchmark session invite.

[21:14] Priya Desai: Thanks.

[21:15] Evan Brooks: Thanks.

[21:16] Sara Kim: Thank you.

[21:18] Markus Klein: Thanks everyone.

[End of transcript excerpt — recording continued with small talk and scheduling logistics]
